c001: Canberra is the capital city of Australia. Located in the Australian Capital Territory, it was purpose-built as the nation's capital, with construction beginning in 1913 after the site was chosen as a compromise between the rival cities of Sydney and Melbourne. The city was designed by the architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, and it is home to Parliament House, the High Court, and many national institutions.
c002: Australia is a country and continent in the Southern Hemisphere, comprising the mainland of the Australian continent, the island of Tasmania, and numerous smaller islands. Although Sydney and Melbourne are its largest and most populous cities, the national capital is Canberra. Australia is known for distinctive wildlife such as kangaroos and koalas, and for natural landmarks including the Great Barrier Reef and Uluru.
c003: The Australian Capital Territory is a federal territory of Australia that contains the national capital, Canberra. The territory was excised from New South Wales in 1911 to provide a neutral location for the new capital. Besides Canberra, the territory includes nature reserves and the small town of Hall. Its government is responsible for local services much like a state government.
c004: The Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait painting by the Italian Renaissance artist Leonardo da Vinci. Painted in the early sixteenth century, it is considered an archetypal masterpiece of the Italian Renaissance and one of the most famous paintings in the world. The subject's enigmatic expression and the artist's use of the sfumato technique have been widely studied, and the painting is held at the Louvre Museum in Paris.
c005: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian polymath of the High Renaissance active as a painter, draughtsman, engineer, scientist, and inventor. Among his best-known works are the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper. Born in 1452 in the town of Vinci, he is widely regarded as one of the greatest painters of all time, and his notebooks reveal a spirit of scientific inquiry centuries ahead of his time.
c006: The Louvre is the world's most-visited museum, located in Paris, France. Originally built as a fortress in the late twelfth century, it became a royal palace before opening as a public museum in 1793. Its collection spans from antiquity to the mid-nineteenth century and includes Leonardo da Vinci's Mona Lisa and the ancient Greek statue Venus de Milo. The glass pyramid in its courtyard was completed in 1989.
c007: Gold is a chemical element with the symbol Au, from the Latin aurum, and atomic number 79. It is a dense, soft, bright yellow metal that is highly malleable and resistant to corrosion. Valued since antiquity for coinage, jewellery, and as a store of value, gold is also used in electronics for its excellent electrical conductivity. Most of the world's gold is mined from deposits in the Earth's crust.
c008: The periodic table is a tabular arrangement of the chemical elements organised by atomic number and recurring chemical properties. Each element is represented by a one- or two-letter symbol, such as H for hydrogen, O for oxygen, Fe for iron, and Au for gold. The table was first published by Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869, who arranged the known elements so that those with similar behaviour fell into the same columns.
c009: Mount Everest is Earth's highest mountain above sea level, with its peak reaching 8,849 metres. It is located in the Mahalangur section of the Himalayas, on the border between Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region of China. The mountain was first summited in 1953 by Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay. Climbers face extreme cold, low oxygen, and dangerous conditions high on its slopes.
c010: The Himalayas are a mountain range in Asia separating the plains of the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau. The range contains many of the Earth's highest peaks, including the very highest, Mount Everest. The Himalayas span five countries and are the source of major rivers such as the Indus and the Ganges. Their formation results from the collision of the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
c011: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun and is often called the Red Planet because of the reddish iron oxide, or rust, that covers much of its surface. It has the largest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons, and a vast canyon system called Valles Marineris. Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos, and has been the target of numerous robotic missions searching for signs of past water and life.
c012: The solar system consists of the Sun and the objects that orbit it, including eight planets. In order from the Sun they are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune. The four inner planets are rocky, while the four outer planets are gas and ice giants. Mars, the fourth planet, is commonly known as the Red Planet, while Jupiter is the largest planet in the system.
c013: Romeo and Juliet is a tragedy written by the English playwright William Shakespeare early in his career. It tells the story of two young star-crossed lovers from feuding families in Verona whose deaths ultimately reconcile their households. The play has been among Shakespeare's most popular works and has been adapted countless times for the stage, film, and opera.
c014: William Shakespeare was an English playwright, poet, and actor widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language. His surviving works include some 39 plays and 154 sonnets. Among his best-known plays are the tragedies Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, Macbeth, and King Lear. Born in Stratford-upon-Avon in 1564, he spent much of his career with the playing company the Lord Chamberlain's Men.
c015: The Pacific Ocean is the largest and deepest of Earth's five oceans. It extends from the Arctic Ocean in the north to the Southern Ocean in the south and is bounded by Asia and Australia in the west and the Americas in the east. It covers about a third of the Earth's surface, more than all the land area combined. Its deepest point, the Challenger Deep, is the deepest known point in any ocean.
c016: Earth's global ocean is divided into five named regions: the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic oceans. The Pacific is by far the largest, followed by the Atlantic and then the Indian Ocean, while the Arctic is the smallest and shallowest. Together the oceans hold about 97 percent of the planet's water and play a central role in regulating climate and weather.
c017: Paris is the capital and most populous city of France, set on the banks of the River Seine in the north of the country. Famous landmarks include the Eiffel Tower, completed in 1889, the Notre-Dame cathedral, and the Arc de Triomphe. A global centre for art, fashion, and culture, Paris draws millions of visitors each year to its museums, grand boulevards, and historic neighbourhoods.
c018: The United States declared independence from Great Britain in 1776, and after the Revolutionary War a new federal government was formed under the Constitution. George Washington, who had commanded the Continental Army, served as the first President of the United States, taking office in 1789. The early republic established institutions such as Congress and the Supreme Court that endure today.
c019: Photosynthesis is the process by which green plants, algae, and some bacteria convert light energy into chemical energy stored in sugars. Using sunlight captured by the pigment chlorophyll, plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil, releasing oxygen as a by-product. This process forms the base of most food chains and is responsible for the oxygen in Earth's atmosphere.
c020: Brazil is the largest country in South America, covering nearly half the continent. Its capital is Brasilia, a planned city inaugurated in 1960, while Sao Paulo and Rio de Janeiro are its largest urban centres. The country is known for the Amazon rainforest, its long Atlantic coastline, and a football culture that has produced many of the sport's most celebrated players.
c021: Water is a chemical substance with the formula H2O, consisting of two hydrogen atoms bonded to one oxygen atom. It covers most of Earth's surface and is essential to all known forms of life, acting as a solvent and a medium for countless biological reactions. Pure water is transparent and nearly colourless, and its unusual properties arise from hydrogen bonding between its molecules.
c022: Canada is the second-largest country in the world by total area, occupying much of northern North America. Its capital is Ottawa, while Toronto, Montreal, and Vancouver are among its largest cities. Canada is officially bilingual in English and French and is known for vast forests, lakes, and Arctic tundra. It shares the world's longest international land border with the United States.
c023: Japan is an island nation in East Asia located in the Pacific Ocean. Its capital is Tokyo, one of the most populous metropolitan areas in the world. Japan comprises four main islands, Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, and Shikoku, along with thousands of smaller ones. It is known for blending ancient traditions with advanced technology and for landmarks such as Mount Fuji.
c024: Egypt is a country linking northeast Africa with the Middle East. Its capital is Cairo, the largest city in the Arab world. Egypt is famous for the ancient civilisation that built the Pyramids of Giza and the Great Sphinx along the Nile River. The Nile, the longest river in Africa, has supported agriculture in the region for thousands of years.
c025: France is a country in Western Europe known for its art, cuisine, and history. Its capital is Paris. The country also includes Mediterranean coastlines in the south, the Alps along its eastern border, and renowned wine regions such as Bordeaux and Burgundy. France is a founding member of the European Union and one of the most visited countries in the world.
c026: The Nile is a major north-flowing river in northeastern Africa, generally regarded as the longest river in Africa. It flows through eleven countries and empties into the Mediterranean Sea. For millennia its annual flooding deposited fertile silt that sustained the civilisations of ancient Egypt. Its two major tributaries, the White Nile and the Blue Nile, meet near the Sudanese capital.
c027: The Amazon is a vast river in South America that carries more water than any other river on Earth. It flows mostly through Brazil and Peru, draining the Amazon rainforest, the largest tropical forest in the world. The river basin is home to an extraordinary diversity of plant and animal species, and its mouth on the Atlantic coast is so wide it resembles an inland sea.
c028: The Atlantic Ocean is the second-largest of the world's oceans, lying between the Americas to the west and Europe and Africa to the east. It has played a central role in human history as a route for exploration, trade, and migration. The mid-Atlantic Ridge, an underwater mountain chain, runs down its length and marks a boundary between tectonic plates.
c029: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system, a gas giant more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. It is known for its Great Red Spot, a giant storm larger than Earth that has raged for centuries. Jupiter has dozens of moons, the four largest of which, Io, Europa, Ganymede, and Callisto, were discovered by Galileo in 1610.
c030: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second-largest in the solar system. It is best known for its spectacular ring system, made up of countless particles of ice and rock. Like Jupiter, Saturn is a gas giant composed mainly of hydrogen and helium. Its largest moon, Titan, has a thick atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane on its surface.
c031: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the hottest in the solar system, wrapped in a thick atmosphere that traps heat in a runaway greenhouse effect. It is similar in size to Earth and is sometimes called Earth's twin. Venus is the brightest natural object in the night sky after the Moon and rotates in the opposite direction to most planets.
c032: Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the only known place in the universe to harbour life. About 71 percent of its surface is covered by water, and its atmosphere is rich in nitrogen and oxygen. Earth has a single natural satellite, the Moon, whose gravitational pull drives the ocean tides, and its rotation gives rise to day and night.
c033: Mercury is the smallest planet in the solar system and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no atmosphere, so its surface experiences extreme temperature swings between scorching days and freezing nights. Heavily cratered, Mercury resembles Earth's Moon in appearance. A single orbit around the Sun takes just 88 Earth days.
c034: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and the fifth-largest moon in the solar system. Its gravitational influence produces the ocean tides and slightly lengthens the day. The Moon's surface is marked by dark plains called maria and bright highlands covered in craters. It always shows the same face to Earth because its rotation period matches its orbital period.
c035: Iron is a chemical element with the symbol Fe and atomic number 26. It is the most common element on Earth by mass, forming much of the planet's outer and inner core. Iron is essential to life as the core of haemoglobin, which carries oxygen in blood. As the main ingredient of steel, it is one of the most widely used metals in construction and manufacturing.
c036: Oxygen is a chemical element with the symbol O and atomic number 8. A colourless, odourless gas, it makes up about 21 percent of Earth's atmosphere and is essential for the respiration of most living things. Oxygen readily forms compounds with most elements, and it is released by plants and algae as a product of photosynthesis. In liquid form it is pale blue.
c037: Hydrogen is the lightest and most abundant chemical element in the universe, with the symbol H and atomic number 1. It is the primary fuel of stars, which shine by fusing hydrogen into helium. On Earth, hydrogen is found mostly bound up in water and organic compounds. As a clean-burning fuel that produces only water when combined with oxygen, it is being explored as an energy carrier.
c038: Helium is a colourless, odourless, inert gas with the symbol He and atomic number 2. It is the second most abundant element in the universe. Lighter than air, helium is used to fill balloons and airships and, in its very cold liquid form, to cool the superconducting magnets of MRI scanners. It was first detected in the spectrum of the Sun before being found on Earth.
c039: Carbon is a chemical element with the symbol C and atomic number 6, and it is the basis of all known life, forming the backbone of organic molecules. Carbon occurs in several forms, including soft graphite and diamond, which is the hardest known natural material. Carbon also cycles through the atmosphere, oceans, and living things in the carbon cycle.
c040: The blue whale is the largest animal known to have ever existed, reaching lengths of up to 30 metres and weights of nearly 200 tonnes. Despite its enormous size, it feeds almost entirely on tiny shrimp-like creatures called krill. Blue whales are found in oceans around the world and communicate using low-frequency calls that can travel for hundreds of kilometres underwater.
c041: The cheetah is the fastest land animal, capable of running at speeds up to about 110 kilometres per hour in short bursts to chase down prey. Native to Africa and a small part of Iran, it has a slender body, long legs, and distinctive black tear marks running from its eyes. Unlike other big cats, the cheetah cannot roar but instead chirps and purrs.
c042: Elephants are the largest living land animals, distinguished by their long trunks, large ears, and tusks. There are three species: the African bush elephant, the African forest elephant, and the Asian elephant. Highly intelligent and social, elephants live in family groups led by an older female, and their trunks contain tens of thousands of muscles used for breathing, grasping, and communication.
c043: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the historical northern borders of China to guard against invasions. Constructed and rebuilt over many centuries, with major work during the Ming dynasty, it stretches for thousands of kilometres. Made of stone, brick, and packed earth, it is one of the most extensive construction projects ever undertaken.
c044: The Roman Empire was one of the largest empires of the ancient world, centred on the city of Rome. At its height it controlled territory around the entire Mediterranean Sea, from Britain to the Middle East. The Romans were renowned for their engineering, including roads, aqueducts, and concrete, and for a system of law that influenced many later legal traditions.
c045: The Pyramids of Giza are ancient monuments built as tombs for the pharaohs of ancient Egypt around 4,500 years ago. The largest, the Great Pyramid, was the tallest human-made structure in the world for thousands of years. Built from millions of limestone blocks, the pyramids stand on the outskirts of Cairo and remain the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still largely intact.
c046: Isaac Newton was an English mathematician and physicist who formulated the laws of motion and universal gravitation in the seventeenth century. His work explained both how objects move on Earth and how planets orbit the Sun under a single set of principles. Newton also made fundamental contributions to optics and, independently of Leibniz, developed the field of calculus.
c047: DNA, or deoxyribonucleic acid, is the molecule that carries the genetic instructions for the development and functioning of living organisms. Its double-helix structure was described by James Watson and Francis Crick in 1953, building on the work of Rosalind Franklin. DNA is made of four chemical bases whose sequence encodes the information needed to build proteins.
c048: Electricity is the set of physical phenomena associated with the presence and motion of electric charge. It powers homes, industry, and electronics, and can be generated from sources such as fossil fuels, nuclear reactions, water, wind, and sunlight. The flow of electric charge through a conductor is called an electric current, measured in amperes.
c049: The Mississippi River is the second-longest river in North America, flowing some 3,700 kilometres from northern Minnesota to the Gulf of Mexico. Together with its tributary the Missouri, it drains a vast basin covering much of the central United States. The river has long been a vital route for transport and trade and features prominently in American literature.
c050: The Danube is the second-longest river in Europe, flowing from Germany's Black Forest eastward through or along ten countries before emptying into the Black Sea. It passes through several capital cities, including Vienna, Budapest, and Belgrade. For centuries the Danube has been an important commercial waterway linking central and southeastern Europe.
c051: The Sahara is the largest hot desert in the world, covering much of North Africa over an area comparable to that of the United States. It is characterised by vast seas of sand dunes, rocky plateaus, and gravel plains, with extreme daytime heat and cold nights. Despite the harsh conditions, the desert supports scattered communities and specially adapted wildlife.
c052: The Alps are the highest and most extensive mountain range lying entirely within Europe, stretching across eight countries. They were formed by the collision of the African and Eurasian tectonic plates. The range is a popular destination for skiing, mountaineering, and hiking, and gives rise to major rivers including the Rhine and the Rhone. Mont Blanc is its highest peak.
c053: K2 is the second-highest mountain on Earth, after Mount Everest, with a summit elevation of 8,611 metres. It lies on the border between Pakistan and China in the Karakoram range. Known for its steepness and severe weather, K2 is considered one of the most difficult and dangerous mountains to climb, earning the nickname the Savage Mountain.
c054: Mount Kilimanjaro is the highest mountain in Africa, rising about 5,895 metres above sea level in Tanzania. A dormant volcano, it stands alone above the surrounding plains and is topped by glaciers that have been shrinking. Because climbers can reach the summit without technical equipment, it is one of the most popular high-altitude treks in the world.
c055: The euro is the official currency of most member states of the European Union, used by more than 340 million people across the eurozone. Introduced as electronic money in 1999 and as cash in 2002, it is managed by the European Central Bank. The euro is one of the world's major reserve currencies, second only to the United States dollar.
c056: The United States dollar is the official currency of the United States and one of the most widely used currencies in the world. It serves as the primary reserve currency held by central banks globally and is used to price many international commodities, including oil and gold. The dollar is divided into 100 cents and is issued by the Federal Reserve.
c057: The Olympic Games are an international sporting event held every four years, alternating between summer and winter editions. Originating in ancient Greece, the modern Games were revived in 1896 and now bring together thousands of athletes from around the world. Events range from athletics and swimming to gymnastics and team sports, and host cities are chosen years in advance.
c058: Spanish is a Romance language that originated in the Iberian Peninsula and is now spoken by hundreds of millions of people, mainly in Spain and across Latin America. It is one of the most widely spoken native languages in the world and an official language of many countries and international organisations. Spanish is written with the Latin alphabet plus a few additional characters.
c059: Mandarin Chinese is the most widely spoken language in the world by number of native speakers. It is the official language of China and Taiwan and one of the official languages of Singapore. Written Chinese uses thousands of characters rather than an alphabet. Mandarin is a tonal language, meaning the pitch used to pronounce a syllable can change its meaning.
c060: Antarctica is Earth's southernmost continent, surrounding the South Pole. It is the coldest, driest, and windiest continent and is almost entirely covered by a thick ice sheet that holds most of the world's fresh water. No permanent human population lives there, but scientists from many countries staff research stations to study the climate, ice, and wildlife such as penguins.
c061: The Sun is the star at the centre of the solar system, a nearly perfect sphere of hot plasma that radiates the energy supporting life on Earth. It generates this energy by fusing hydrogen into helium in its core. Accounting for about 99.8 percent of the mass of the solar system, the Sun's gravity holds the planets in their orbits.
c062: The Internet is a global network of interconnected computer networks that communicate using standard protocols. It grew out of research projects in the late twentieth century and now underpins the World Wide Web, email, and countless online services. Data is broken into packets and routed across the network, allowing computers around the world to exchange information almost instantly.
c063: A volcano is a rupture in the crust of a planet that allows molten rock, ash, and gases to escape from below the surface. On Earth, volcanoes are often found where tectonic plates meet. Eruptions can be explosive or gentle, building mountains and islands over time. The study of volcanoes, volcanology, helps scientists forecast eruptions and reduce risk to nearby communities.
c064: Coffee is a brewed drink prepared from the roasted seeds of the Coffea plant, native to tropical Africa. After being cultivated and traded for centuries, it is now one of the most popular beverages in the world. Major producers include Brazil, Colombia, and Ethiopia, and the drink is valued for the stimulant effect of its caffeine.
c065: Tea is an aromatic beverage made by pouring hot water over cured or fresh leaves of the plant Camellia sinensis. Originating in East Asia, it is the most widely consumed drink in the world after water. Varieties such as green, black, and oolong differ mainly in how the leaves are processed, and tea is traditionally central to the cultures of China, Japan, and India.
c066: Penguins are a group of flightless seabirds found almost exclusively in the Southern Hemisphere, especially around Antarctica. Their wings have evolved into flippers that make them strong swimmers, and their black-and-white plumage camouflages them in the water. Penguins gather in large colonies to breed and huddle together to keep warm in harsh climates.
c067: The lion is a large cat native to Africa and a small population in India. Often called the king of beasts, it lives in social groups called prides, typically made up of related females, their cubs, and a few adult males. Male lions are recognisable by their manes, and lions are apex predators that hunt large herbivores cooperatively on the savanna.
c068: Sharks are a group of fish characterised by skeletons made of cartilage rather than bone. They have existed for hundreds of millions of years, predating the dinosaurs. Ranging from the small dwarf lanternshark to the enormous whale shark, sharks occupy many ocean habitats. Most species pose no threat to humans and play an important role as predators in marine ecosystems.
c069: Bees are flying insects known for their role in pollination and, in some species, for producing honey and beeswax. The best-known species is the western honey bee, which lives in large colonies with a single queen. As bees move between flowers to collect nectar, they transfer pollen, fertilising plants and supporting the production of many fruits and crops.
c070: A tropical rainforest is a dense forest found in regions of high rainfall and warm temperatures near the equator. Rainforests host more than half of the world's plant and animal species despite covering a small fraction of its land. They play a vital role in regulating the global climate by storing carbon and producing oxygen, and the Congo and the Amazon basins are among the largest.
c071: The camel is a large mammal adapted to life in deserts, able to go for long periods without water. The dromedary has a single hump and the Bactrian camel has two; the humps store fat rather than water. Camels have long been used by desert peoples for transport, milk, and wool, earning the nickname ships of the desert.
c072: A telescope is an instrument that gathers and magnifies light to make distant objects appear closer and brighter. The first practical telescopes appeared in the early seventeenth century, and Galileo used one to observe the moons of Jupiter and the phases of Venus. Modern telescopes, including giant ground-based observatories and space telescopes, have transformed our understanding of the universe.
c073: A vaccine is a biological preparation that trains the immune system to recognise and fight a specific disease without causing the illness itself. Vaccines have dramatically reduced the burden of infectious diseases such as smallpox, declared eradicated in 1980, and polio. They typically contain a weakened, inactivated, or partial form of a pathogen.
c074: A suspension bridge is a type of bridge in which the deck hangs below suspension cables supported by towers. This design allows for very long spans across wide rivers or bays. Famous examples include the Golden Gate Bridge in San Francisco and the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge in Japan. The main cables carry the load in tension to anchorages at each end.
c075: A computer is a machine that can be programmed to carry out sequences of arithmetic or logical operations automatically. Modern computers are built around integrated circuits and can store and process vast amounts of data. They range from tiny embedded controllers to powerful supercomputers and underpin communications, science, business, and entertainment around the world.
c076: Chocolate is a food made from the roasted and ground seeds of the cacao tree, which is native to the tropical Americas. The seeds, or cocoa beans, were used by ancient Mesoamerican cultures to make a bitter drink. Today chocolate is produced in many forms, often with sugar and milk added, and West Africa supplies most of the world's cocoa.
